name: Andromeda Galaxy
gases: Hydrogen, Helium, trace amounts of metals.
facts: The largest galaxy in the Local Group.
It is on a collision course with the Milky Way, expected in about 4.5 billion years.
The most distant object visible to the naked eye.

name: Orion Nebula
gases: Ionized Hydrogen, Oxygen, Sulfur.
facts: A massive stellar nursery where new stars are actively being formed.
Contains the Trapezium cluster, a tight grouping of young, hot stars.
One of the brightest nebulae and easy to spot in the winter sky.

name: Pleiades Cluster
gases: Interstellar dust and gas (mainly Hydrogen).
facts: Also known as the Seven Sisters.
An open star cluster dominated by hot, blue luminous stars.
Used as a time marker by ancient cultures worldwide.

name: Crab Nebula
gases: Hydrogen, Helium, traces of heavier elements (e.g., Oxygen, Neon).
facts: A supernova remnant resulting from an explosion observed in 1054 AD.
Contains a pulsar (a rapidly spinning neutron star) at its center.

name: Whirlpool Galaxy
gases: Hydrogen, Molecular clouds, Carbon Monoxide.
facts: One of the most famous examples of a grand-design spiral galaxy.
It is currently interacting and merging with its smaller neighbor, NGC 5195.

name: Ring Nebula
gases: Oxygen (green), Nitrogen (red), Helium.
facts: A classic example of a planetary nebula, the final stage of a Sun-like star.
The "smoke ring" appearance is caused by a shell of gas ejected from the central white dwarf.

name: Hercules Globular Cluster
gases: Extremely low concentration; mainly very old, dense stars.
facts: One of the most spectacular globular clusters in the Northern Hemisphere.
Contains several hundred thousand stars tightly bound by gravity.

name: Lagoon Nebula
gases: Ionized Hydrogen, dust, and dark lanes of dust (the 'Lagoon').
facts: A large interstellar cloud in the constellation Sagittarius.
Visible to the naked eye under dark skies due to its size.

name: Triangulum Galaxy
gases: Hydrogen, Helium, active star-forming regions (H II regions).
facts: The third-largest galaxy in the Local Group (after Andromeda and the Milky Way).
It is a face-on spiral, making its structure difficult to see but its overall size impressive.

name: Swan Nebula
gases: Hydrogen, Sulfur, Oxygen.
facts: Named for its resemblance to a swan or checkmark shape.
One of the most active and massive star-forming regions in our galaxy.

name: Pinwheel Galaxy
gases: Primarily Hydrogen and Helium in arms.
facts: A large, beautiful face-on spiral galaxy in the constellation Ursa Major.
It hosts exceptionally large and bright H II regions (star-forming areas).

name: Owl Nebula
gases: Oxygen (central region), Hydrogen (outer shell).
facts: A planetary nebula named for its two dark, owl-like 'eyes'.
It is faint and requires a large telescope and dark skies to observe well.

name: Coma Cluster
gases: Massive amounts of X-ray-emitting intergalactic gas.
facts: One of the nearest rich clusters of galaxies to the Milky Way.
Contains thousands of galaxies, mostly ellipticals.

name: Dumbbell Nebula
gases: Ionized Helium, Hydrogen, Nitrogen.
facts: The first planetary nebula ever discovered (by Charles Messier in 1764).
The nebula appears brighter and more colorful in telescopes than most planetary nebulae.

name: Sombrero Galaxy
gases: Dust lane rich in molecular gas.
facts: Named for its resemblance to a wide-brimmed hat.
Has an unusually large and bright central bulge.

name: Jewel Box Cluster
gases: Very young, hot star environment.
facts: One of the youngest known open clusters, located in the Southern Cross.
Features contrasting colors: brilliant blue, white, and red stars.

name: Veil Nebula
gases: Oxygen, Hydrogen, Sulfur (expanding supernova shock wave).
facts: Part of the much larger Cygnus Loop supernova remnant.
The entire structure spans over 6 times the diameter of the full Moon.

name: Bode's Galaxy
gases: Cold molecular gas clouds.
facts: A grand spiral galaxy visible with binoculars in dark skies.
Forms a famous pair with its smaller, distorted neighbor, M82.

name: Cigar Galaxy
gases: Reddish Hydrogen filaments being violently ejected.
facts: A spectacular starburst galaxy, forming stars ten times faster than the Milky Way.
Its shape is distorted due to gravitational interaction with M81.

name: Bubble Nebula
gases: Stellar wind-shocked Hydrogen and Oxygen.
facts: The "bubble" is caused by intense stellar wind from a massive, hot central star.
The star generating the bubble is about 45 times the mass of the Sun.

name: Omega Centauri
gases: Very little gas; remnant of a small galaxy.
facts: The largest and brightest globular cluster known in the Milky Way.
Believed to be the core remnant of a dwarf galaxy absorbed by our own.

name: Small Magellanic Cloud
gases: Large amounts of neutral Hydrogen gas (H I).
facts: A dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, only visible from the Southern Hemisphere.
It is tidally disrupted, showing a distorted, irregular shape.

name: Horsehead Nebula
gases: Cold dust and dense Hydrogen gas (appears dark).
facts: A dark nebula that gets its shape from being silhouetted against a bright emission nebula.
It is part of the much larger Orion Molecular Cloud Complex.

name: Eskimo Nebula
gases: Oxygen (inner ring), Nitrogen/Hydrogen (outer filaments).
facts: A planetary nebula with two elliptical rings resembling a face surrounded by a fur hood.
The inner ring is expanding at about 60,000 km/h.

name: Carina Nebula
gases: Ionized Hydrogen, molecular clouds, dark dust.
facts: One of the largest diffuse nebulae in the sky, much larger than the Orion Nebula.
Home to the massive, unstable star Eta Carinae.
